title: Reasoning's Razor: Reasoning Improves Accuracy but Can Hurt Recall at Critical Operating Points in Safety and Hallucination Detection
authors: Atoosa Chegini; Hamid Kazemi; Garrett Souza; Maria Safi; Yang Song; Samy Bengio; et al.
manipulation: Think On vs Think Off on the same model (reasoning section before verdict for LLMs; empty thinking tags for LRMs); fine-tuned vs zero-shot; certainty-level prompts ('at least X% certain', X = 60-99)
measurement: Token-based scores (normalized label-token logits) vs verbalized 0-100 confidence; ROC; TPR at fixed low FPR (e.g. 1%); accuracy
domain_models: Safety detection (ToxicChat, OpenAI Moderation, Aegis, WildGuardTest, HarmBench, SafeRLHF, BeaverTails, XSTest) and RAG hallucination detection (HaluBench); Llama-3 1B/8B, Qwen2.5 7B/14B/32B, QwQ-32B, R1-distill-Qwen32B, K2-Think, GuardReasoner-tuned Llama-8B, Lynx 8B/70B
notes: Read via WebFetch (methods and results; first 100k of 112k chars). Thinking raises accuracy but lowers TPR at 1% FPR (fine-tuned safety model 40.0% Off vs 13.8% On); token scores beat verbalized ones at strict operating points (QwQ-32B 30.6% vs 10.0%), verbal scores often degenerate. Certainty prompts move Think On operating points (21.5% -> 40.1%). Partly covers C7 (verdict-token ROC for LLM detectors) and touches C8 (thinking changes operating characteristics); no base rate, payoff or ideal observer; no clear size trend. [arXiv versions seen: v1]
